articles.headline: Microsoft Scientist Calls News Scraping Historic Labor Theft
articles.deck: An unsealed summary judgment motion from plaintiffs led by The New York Times cites internal warnings about substitution, traffic losses and verbatim outputs.

pullquote.text: largest theft of labor in human history

body: An unsealed motion for summary judgment from news plaintiffs led by The New York Times presents internal Microsoft and OpenAI documents that describe training AI on news content as theft that threatens publishers and weakens fair use claims. Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht called scraping news for AI training “largest theft of labor in human history” and “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”. ChatGPT head Nick Turley wrote that publishers faced an “existential threat” from products that substitute for news providers.

One Microsoft document described a “doom loop” that will hurt model performance and the web at the same time, warning that an end product threatened the economic foundations of its essential suppliers. Microsoft recorded 83 to 93 percent drops in click through rates for some news plaintiffs and 51 to 94 percent drops for others. OpenAI staff agreed users will not click through when chatbots supply answers directly.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified under oath that AI companies should not violate news sites terms of use by dodging paywalls and described chatbots as substitutes that keep users from visiting sources. An OpenAI staffer told President Greg Brockman about a hack to get around the NYT paywall, and Brockman replied “Ah, nice”. News groups tested chatbot outputs by requesting summaries, bullet points and bias ratings and found excerpts reproduced verbatim.

News plaintiffs now seek a ruling only on infringed articles where outputs show “extensive verbatim overlap” and argue substitution weighs against fair use. A Microsoft spokesperson called the products transformative fair use that do not substitute for news sites and said Hecht documents reflect “one employee’s individual perspective”. Counsel for the New York Daily News said the documents show Microsoft and OpenAI knew their conduct was wrong and kept the records confidential from public view until now.

art.caption: A federal courthouse with stone steps and columns. The Times-led plaintiffs ask the court to rule that chatbot outputs with extensive verbatim overlap infringe copyright.

articles.headline: EU proposal gates social media behind age checks
articles.deck: Phased accounts for teenagers and safety rules for AI and games would expand verification to all users.

pullquote.text: However they’re designed, age gates undermine civil liberties, reduce safety, and create barriers to internet entry, often at the expense of marginalized groups.

body: The EU Commission has proposed a law that would place social media and AI systems behind age gates. The draft sets phased access for young people and requires verification that critics say would reduce privacy for all users. The Electronic Frontier Foundation says the measure trades safety for surveillance infrastructure.

Platforms with personalized recommender systems or uninterrupted content consumption would face the strictest tiers. Children under 13 would have no service accounts. Teenagers from 13 to 15 would have restricted accounts under tight parental supervision. Teenagers from 15 to 18 would have autonomous accounts in a safe by design environment. Full online access would remain reserved for adults.

The access delay would rely on the EU age verification scheme. Parents would set up accounts for teenagers and prove parental status. That adds a second layer of identity checks. Existing accounts could avoid checks only if a provider can show with high degree of confidence that the user is above the threshold. The standard for that confidence remains vaguely specified.

A second pillar called safety by design would cover social media, video sharing, online games, AI companions, chatbots and app stores. Providers would make child safe design the default and relax rules only after age assurance shows the user is an adult. Rules address infinite scrolling, account settings and choice over recommender systems. AI companions would face limits to reduce emotional dependencies and harmful interactions. Games would need contact protections. App stores would enforce age appropriate access through an age rating system.

Exemptions would apply to not for profit encyclopedias, scientific repositories, educational services and open source software platforms. No exemption would apply to small and medium sized enterprises. Critics say that gap would favor large technology companies with compliance resources and push others toward strict checks by default. They also warn that age thresholds are a blunt proxy for maturity, that broad coverage would affect almost all mainstream services, and that the focus on harms gives little weight to privacy, freedom of expression and the right of children to seek information and take part online.

The draft builds on the Digital Services Act and turns non binding guidance on minors into hard rules. Its backers cite proportionality compared with a blanket ban rejected by a French court last month. Critics cite problems for decentralized networks, prior compliance plans for very large platforms, and the absence of an impact assessment. They urge lawmakers to remove the harmful parts. The teeth remain sharp for now.

articles.headline: Muse Tops ChatGPT in Early iOS Downloads
articles.deck: Apptopia puts Muse at 1.8 million iOS downloads against 1.3 million for ChatGPT in the United States and Canada during the first 12 days.
body: Estimates from Apptopia show the Muse app from Meta recorded 1.8 million iOS downloads in the United States and Canada during its first 12 days on the market, compared with 1.3 million for ChatGPT over the same period after its debut.

The comparison covers iOS in the United States and Canada only. ChatGPT launched globally on iOS only. Muse launched in the United States and Canada on iOS and Android. Apptopia limited the comparison to the same stores and markets to align the figures. Total installs of Muse reached 2.8 million globally in the first 12 days.

Daily active users in the United States also favor Muse. Apptopia reports 642,000 daily users for Muse against 231,000 for ChatGPT at the same point after launch. On iOS alone, Apptopia reports 359,000 daily active users in the United States, still above the ChatGPT figure for that period. Muse rose from No. 2 to No. 1 on the United States App Store after launch, ahead of ChatGPT, according to Business Insider. Appfigures said Muse had crossed 1 million downloads at that time.

Apptopia cautions that its figures are third party estimates without direct access to internal figures from Meta. Meta has not shared public figures related to early adoption of Muse. The report notes overlap with existing Meta services. More than 95 percent of Muse users also use Facebook, and 63 percent also use Instagram. Muse connects with Instagram and Facebook and also works inside WhatsApp. Meta used heavy marketing and integrations across Instagram and Facebook for Threads, which now has more than 500 million users. Apptopia has no direct visibility into cross promotion or ads for Muse. Growth had not stagnated during the period covered by the estimates. The figures describe early use only at this stage.

articles.headline: Ninth Circuit Rejects DMCA Claim Against AI
articles.deck: Anonymous Github contributors said model output copied their code without copyright notices.
body: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected a claim that makers of large language models violated Section 1202 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act by training on code without copyright management information. Anonymous Github contributors sued Open AI and Microsoft over training data taken from Github. The court held that creating a new work without such information is different from removing it from an existing work.

Section 1202 prohibits intentional removal of copyright management information such as an author name or copyright notice. The plaintiffs alleged output code resembled their code but lacked that information. The court said absence of information in a new work does not by itself prove unlawful removal. Copyright infringement claims remain available where a model reproduces protected code. Contract claims against the companies also remain in play.

The decision limits a theory that could have exposed lawful users to costly suits. The Electronic Frontier Foundation warned that artists making remixes, teachers adapting works for classroom presentation, engineers reverse engineering code, and search engines could have faced claims. Independent software developers faced particular risk from federal litigation and statutory damages. Large companies can sustain prolonged defense. An independent programmer might settle despite lawful use. The ruling keeps Section 1202 as a backstop for traditional rights rather than a broad restriction on noninfringing use. New technologies will continue to raise questions under rights Congress authorized without new restrictions.

articles.headline: MIT methodologist sharpens tools to measure politics accurately
articles.deck: Naoki Egami studies external validity, AI measurement and campaign experiments.

pullquote.text: You find out the underlying mathematical problems behind the empirical challenges people face, and solve them optimally.

body: Naoki Egami builds statistical tools to measure social and political phenomena with precision. The MIT political scientist specializes in methodology and external validity. His research asks whether results from one study apply in other settings. His projects include field experiments in campaigns and measurement with artificial intelligence tools. He joined the Department of Political Science as an associate professor with tenure in 2025. He teaches undergraduate and graduate classes.

Egami is also a faculty affiliate of the Statistics and Data Science Center at the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society. His work identifies mathematical problems behind empirical challenges and solves them optimally. He combines questions from political science with methods from applied statistics and computer science. The approach pairs substantive problems with technical solutions. Technical theory alone can miss interesting problems. Problem focus alone can lead to ad-hoc solutions. “You need both perspectives,” Egami says.

Field experiments in active campaigns illustrate the problem. Politicians sometimes grant researchers access to campaigns they expect to win. Politicians know they can win in those settings. Voter behavior in those lopsided races can differ from behavior in competitive districts. Findings from lopsided races may not transfer to battlefield races. Egami scrutinizes such differences in context. Statistics considers similarity of populations. Political science must also account for differences in context.

Before the current artificial intelligence interest, Egami studied accuracy when AI tools enter studies. He asks how accurate the tools are and how researchers can account for their tendencies. The work helped build a broad portfolio and win awards. He retains interest in basic questions about politics. He starts new research agendas every three to four years to learn new topics. Motivation grows with new topics.

Egami grew up in Tokyo and attended the University of Tokyo. He was good at math and physics and liked political philosophy. He attended a workshop about U.S. graduate school with 200 people. A doctoral student panelist found him after the session. She invited him to a seminar the following week. The room held 20 people, including 19 professors. Kosuke Imai spoke about statistics in social science.

Egami spent a year as an exchange student at the University of Michigan and received his BA. He earned his PhD from Princeton University in 2020. He worked with Kosuke Imai, Rafaela Dancygier, Brandon Stewart and others on external validity. He presented papers and found substantial interest. He joined the faculty at Columbia University. He moved to MIT five years later. The path reflects preparation meeting opportunity.

articles.headline: Boston Drops Flock After Nationwide Data Sharing
articles.deck: A three-day pilot error exposed plate records, yet the city started trials with two other vendors.

pullquote.text: When the toggles or the access controls either are not able to be restricted in the ways that conform with that policy, or are set but then can be unset or reset in ways that violate that policy, we would not use that platform.

body: Boston ended its trial of Flock Safety license plate cameras after the company shared department data with law enforcement agencies across the country. The sharing violated a contract that limited access to trained Boston Police Department personnel. Mayor Michelle Wu confirmed the decision last week.

The department deployed about 45 automated license plate reader cameras from April to September last year. Within three days, officers learned outside agencies could view plate and vehicle records through a nationwide lookup feature. The company had enabled the feature in error after confirming sharing settings were off. The department disabled direct access and required written requests for the rest of the trial.

The annual surveillance technology report covering 2025 did not state how many agencies viewed the records. The city requires vendors to block sharing and erase recordings after 30 days unless police retain video for legal or investigative purposes. The department began a trial with Motorola in February 2026 and a third trial with Axon in June 2026.

The report arrived during a debate over police use of plate data. An Electronic Frontier Foundation analysis of search logs said officers across the country run searches without legitimate justification and log nonsensical reasons. Flock Safety said it improved its system by requiring officers to select a crime from a dropdown list before a search. The foundation said the system in place since late 2025 does not require proof the reason matches the true purpose. Wu said the city needs an approved policy to protect privacy and civil liberties before deploying tools to keep people safe and solve crimes faster. She said the department is testing versions to track movement and must know who can access data and how long it is stored. The company said new partnerships in 2026 outpaced nonrenewals by 10 to 1.

art.caption: A surveillance camera watches a city street from a pole. Boston ended its Flock license-plate trial after a sharing error.

articles.headline: AI PACs pour cash into South Dakota Senate race
articles.deck: Incumbent Mike Rounds leads a noncompetitive contest drawing outside money tied to AI labs and investors.
body: Major super PACs tied to AI labs and investors have poured close to $1 million into the South Dakota Senate race of incumbent Republican Mike Rounds. The spending targets a noncompetitive contest with fewer than 50 days until the midterm elections in November. Recent polls show Rounds ahead of independent candidate Brian Beng after Democratic candidate Julian Beaudion dropped out last month.

Rounds has been the beneficiary this cycle of around $600,000 in spending by outside groups. The vast majority of that figure comes from the super PAC Defend American Jobs. That group receives funding from a super PAC financed by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

He has also received roughly $215,000 directly from employees and super PACs affiliated with AI labs. The labs include most notably Anthropic. Other tech companies include Google and Microsoft, according to FEC filings. Rounds has so far raised more from tech groups than from donors in South Dakota.

AI executives view Rounds as a top supporter of the industry. The support could prove crucial in the next Congress when AI regulation is expected to become a top priority, according to congressional aides familiar with the matter. The spending reflects a new effort by AI labs to deploy vast war chests to shape issues on AI and the data centers that power it.

AI labs have focused on keeping allies in short supply on Capitol Hill as lawmakers react to public anxiety around AI safety concerns. On Thursday, Leading the Future announced it would put $2 million towards a raft of Senate Republicans supportive of the AI or crypto industry. The super PAC is funded in part by OpenAI president Greg Brockman, along with investors Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreesen. The list included Rounds.

In South Dakota, AI regulation is already a live issue after the state legislature passed a bill earlier this year forcing hyperscalers to bear a larger share of the water and energy costs associated with powering data centers. The state legislature voted against giving tax breaks for equipment and software purchases required by data centers earlier this year, stalling construction of a planned development by Applied Digital, a company that builds and designs data centers. Rounds ultimately endorsed adding restrictions on data centers. His senior aide and former chief of staff, Robert Skjonsberg, is a registered lobbyist for Meta for matters before the South Dakota legislature. A recent Gallup poll found that seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to data center development.

articles.headline: MIT Reads Turns to Fiction for Tenth Anniversary
articles.deck: President Sally Kornbluth has selected Exhalation by Ted Chiang for fall 2026 to open the focus on fiction and memoir.

pullquote.text: Reading together also gives us the increasingly rare opportunity for both individual reflection and shared connection.

body: MIT Reads will mark ten years by turning to fiction and memoir. The MIT Libraries program links the shift to artificial intelligence and the need for social connection and shared humanity. President Sally Kornbluth has selected Exhalation by Ted Chiang as the fall 2026 book. The choice signals a focus on stories and their power to clarify ourselves and our place in the world.

Launched in 2016, MIT Reads was designed to foster empathy, understanding and belonging within the campus community. Each selected book is accompanied by talks by the featured author, panel discussions and small group conversations facilitated by library staff. Program leaders say the value of collective reading, reflection and discussion has never been more relevant.

MIT Libraries Director Chris Bourg links fiction to the work of building for the future. He describes reading together as a rare opportunity for individual reflection and shared connection. The program is evolving as MIT examines AI influence on the education landscape and the social fabric of the Institute. A report from the Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training urges stronger social connection and cites MIT Reads as a path forward.

Exhalation is a bestselling collection of short stories. It was named one of The New York Times best books of 2019. Chiang builds scenarios with robots, time travel and alternate universes. The stories explore identity, free will, language and the impacts of technology. Kornbluth describes the collection as a preview of current questions about technology and the relationship between humans and artificial intelligence.

Most author events are open to the public and streamed online. Videos of MIT Reads talks have been viewed more than 5,000 times. Bourg invites readers everywhere to join the wider discussion of technology and humanity. Students in the first year advising seminar 21.A01 will read Exhalation this fall. The class is part of the Compass initiative designed by faculty from across the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences.

The Compass course carries the full title Reading Great Books with Compass. It has support from the MIT Human Insight Collaborative. The connection places fiction inside first year advising and humanities teaching. Organizers frame stories as a way to understand ourselves and our place in the world. The fall book raises deep questions about the future that humans and machines will share. It offers provocative ideas and possibilities for discussion. The rest is reading. Readers everywhere are invited to join the conversation starting with Exhalation.
